html:
Corps of women soldiers in the army of the West African kingdom of Dahomey, active from about 1700 until the French conquest in 1894. Europeans called them Amazons. In the Fon language they were the Agojie or Mino, "our mothers".

They are thought to have begun as royal bodyguards and elephant hunters, and grew into a regular force under kings such as agaja, who ruled in the early 1700s. By the 1800s women may have made up as much as a third of the army, though counts are rough. They lived in the palace, trained hard, and were sworn to the king.

They fought Dahomey's neighbours, including oyo, and raided for captives who were sold into the atlantic-slave-trade, which paid for the state. Under ghezo and later kings they were feared by European visitors.

Their last fights were against the French, in the first-franco-dahomean-war of 1890 and the war of 1892 to 1894. Rifles and artillery beat them, and behanzin surrendered in 1894.
sum: Corps of women soldiers in the army of the West African kingdom of Dahomey, active from about 1700 until the French conquest in 1894. Europeans called them Amazons. In the Fon language they were the Agojie or Mino, "our mothers".
